title: Ten minutes of learning
hook: a fixed daily time for study, however short (Avot 1:15)
tomorrow: Isaac walked out into a field at dusk. to do what, exactly?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pushke: one coin, again and again, until giving is part of you. A coin a week. Today, the same idea, with time instead of money.

A calendar fills up from the outside in: other people's meetings, practices, appointments, and whatever's left over is yours, if anything is. The Talmud has a surprising worry about that. In its picture of the end of a life, when a person stands to give an account, the questions are practical. One of them is about your calendar. It doesn't ask how much you knew. It asks whether you set a time. Why would that be the question?
screen: `A CALENDAR FILLS FROM THE OUTSIDE IN.` → `THE QUESTIONS AT THE END.` → `ONE IS ABOUT YOUR CALENDAR.`

segments.voice: The sage Rava lists the questions a person is asked. Did you deal honestly in business? Did you fix times for Torah? Not how much you learned, or how clever you got. Whether you fixed the time. The word is kavata, from keva, something fixed and set. It echoes Shammai in Pirkei Avot: make your study a fixed thing. Hillel, his famous partner in argument, says why it matters: don't say, when I have free time I'll study, because maybe you'll never have free time. Anyone who has waited for a free afternoon knows how that goes. A fixed time doesn't wait for the mood or an empty calendar. It's an appointment, and you show up on the thin days too. So how long does it have to be? The Talmud records a generous answer. One sage says a chapter in the morning and a chapter in the evening keeps the verse, "This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth." Another goes further: even the Shema, said morning and evening, counts. So a tradition with long nights of study also leaves the door open to ten minutes. The size can be small. The time has to be real. Something to tell a friend tonight: the question isn't how much you learned. It's whether you fixed a time.
screen: `DID YOU FIX TIMES FOR TORAH?` · `KEVA: MAKE IT A FIXED THING.` · `DON'T WAIT FOR FREE TIME.` · `A CHAPTER MORNING AND EVENING.` · then, large: `FIX A TIME.`

segments.voice: Choose your ten minutes now, and hang them on something that already happens: after coffee, on the bus, before the phone at night. Say the plan to yourself plainly: when this happens, I open the book. Then decide what you'll read first, so tomorrow begins without deciding.
screen: `HANG IT ON SOMETHING THAT ALREADY HAPPENS.` · `WHEN THIS HAPPENS, I OPEN THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: Ten minutes of learning: a short time for study, fixed like an appointment, kept on busy days and thin ones.
Here's the line: fix a time. The amount can be small; the appointment is real.

screen: `DAY 1654 COUNTS.` → `A RULE OF LIFE · 7 OF 15.` → `TOMORROW: ISAAC IN A FIELD AT DUSK. DOING WHAT?`

howItsDone: Some Jews keep a set daily study time: a page of Talmud, a chapter of Mishnah, the week's Torah portion, or a short daily study cycle, alone, with a study partner, or by phone with a teacher. Synagogues often hold a short study session between the afternoon and evening prayers.

chat.meaning: Hillel warns that free time may never come, and the Talmud asks whether you fixed times, not how much. Ten fixed minutes count.

Rava.meaning: a sage of the Babylonian Talmud

Shammai.meaning: a sage of the Mishnah, often paired with Hillel

Hillel.meaning: a sage of the Mishnah, Shammai's partner in argument

Shema.meaning: the line 'Hear, O Israel,' said morning and evening

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a (Rava: the questions a person is asked, including 'did you fix times for Torah?')
Mishnah Avot 1:15 (Shammai: make your Torah study fixed)
Mishnah Avot 2:4 (Hillel: do not say 'when I have leisure I will study')

sources.quoted: This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth

notes: Shabbat 31a: the order of Rava's questions (business first, then fixed times for Torah) as the script implies by listing them together; confirm.

Menachot 99b: Rabbi Ammi (a chapter morning and evening) and Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai (even the Shema); names left out of the voice. Confirm attribution and the Joshua 1:8 wording in JPS 1917.
Avot 2:4 is commonly numbered 2:5 in some editions; confirm numbering.
'Hillel, his famous partner in argument': 'famous' is soft praise, not a counted claim; editor may cut.
